title: "9. Reconciling the density literature"
subtitle: "Within-place evidence compared with the multiverse; cross-sectional studies as descriptive context"
execute:
  echo: false

```{r}
#| label: matrix-helpers
library( data.table )
rd <- function( f ) fread( file.path( "data", f ), encoding = "UTF-8", colClasses = "character", na.strings = character( 0 ) )
norm <- function( x ) gsub( "-", "−", x, fixed = TRUE )
## one coloured cell; implicit tests (theory table) are shown in parentheses
cell <- function( x ) {
  x <- norm( x ); if ( !nzchar( x ) ) return( "" )
  impl <- startsWith( x, "I" ); s <- sub( "^[EI]", "", x )
  cls <- switch( s, "+" = "r-pos", "−" = "r-neg", "0" = "r-null", "±" = "r-mix", "r-null" )
  lab <- if ( impl ) paste0( "(", s, ")" ) else s
  sprintf( "[%s]{.%s}", lab, cls )
}
MV_LABELS <- c( "MV-w-filers" = "Multiverse within metros: filers",
                "MV-w-grassroots" = "Multiverse within metros: grassroots",
                "MV-w-spending" = "Multiverse within metros: spending",
                "MV-w" = "Multiverse within metros" )
label <- function( key, group, read ) {
  if ( group == "multiverse" ) return( sprintf( "**%s**", MV_LABELS[[ key ]] ) )
  paste0( "@", key, if ( read == "abstract" ) "\\*" else "" )
}
## agreement verdict across studies (multiverse rows excluded)
verdict <- function( v ) {
  v <- sub( "^[EI]", "", norm( v[ nzchar( v ) ] ) ); n <- length( v ); if ( !n ) return( c( "", "", "" ) )
  p <- sum( v == "+" ); m <- sum( v == "−" ); z <- sum( v == "0" ); x <- sum( v == "±" )
  dom <- if ( p >= m ) "+" else "−"; share <- max( p, m ) / n
  ver <- if ( n < 2 ) "one study" else if ( share >= .7 ) paste0( "agree (", dom, ")" ) else
         if ( p > 0 && m > 0 && min( p, m ) / max( p, m ) >= .5 ) "diverge" else
         if ( share >= .5 ) paste0( "lean (", dom, ")" ) else "mixed"
  cls <- if ( startsWith( ver, "agree" ) ) "r-pos" else if ( ver == "diverge" ) "r-neg" else "r-mix"
  c( as.character( n ), sprintf( "%d / %d / %d / %d", p, m, z, x ), sprintf( "[%s]{.%s}", ver, cls ) )
}
matrix_md <- function( d, cols, heads ) {
  body <- d[ , c( list( Study = mapply( label, key, group, read ) ), lapply( .SD, function( v ) vapply( v, cell, "" ) ) ), .SDcols = cols ]
  setnames( body, c( "Study", heads ) )
  st <- d[ group != "multiverse" ]
  summ <- lapply( cols, function( cc ) verdict( st[[ cc ]] ) )
  extra <- data.table( Study = c( "*Studies testing*", "*+ / − / 0 / ±*", "*Agreement*" ) )
  for ( i in seq_along( cols ) ) extra[[ heads[ i ] ]] <- summ[[ i ]]
  out <- rbind( body, extra )
  cat( knitr::kable( out, format = "pipe", align = c( "l", rep( "c", length( cols ) ) ) ), sep = "\n" )
}
notes_md <- function( d ) {
  d <- d[ nzchar( note ) ]
  cat( paste0( "- ", mapply( label, d$key, d$group, d$read ), ": ", gsub( "-", "−", d$note, fixed = TRUE ) ), sep = "\n" )
}
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Draft, 2026-11-18.** The data, models and results of the studies are taken from
their full published texts, except where a table marks a study as abstract only.

**How this page weighs evidence.**

- **Within-place designs carry the weight.** These are panels with unit fixed effects,
  which compare each place with itself over time, much like a difference-in-
  differences design.
- **Cross-sectional studies are descriptive.** They describe *where* nonprofits are,
  not what changes their number, so they appear in a separate section and are not
  used to adjudicate claims.

The mapping of each study onto the multiverse decisions is ours. It is an argument,
not a re-estimation of their models.
:::

# The question

Local foundations and governments want to know what *changes* the size of a
nonprofit sector. Most density studies cannot answer that, because they compare
different places at one point in time, and places differ in ways no model fully
captures:

- history;
- regional culture;
- the legacy of earlier institutions.

A within-place design asks a narrower but more useful question: when conditions in a
place change, does its nonprofit sector change with them? With unit and year fixed
effects, every place serves as its own control, and shocks common to all places are
removed.

This page therefore compares within-place results with within-place results:

- **The literature's panel studies** with fixed effects.
- **The multiverse's within-metro estimates:** metro and year fixed effects,
  2010–2022, for filers, grassroots and spending.

Cross-sectional studies follow in a descriptive section. They are useful for
describing levels and gaps, but not for settling what drives change.

# The studies by design

Of the 36 studies reviewed, six estimate within-place models. The rest are
cross-sections, pooled cross-sections, or random-effects panels, whose estimates are
dominated by differences between places.

::: {.table-compact}

| Design | What it compares | Studies |
|---|---|---|
| **Within (unit fixed effects)** | Each place with itself over time | @matsunaga2004government (state and year FE); @lecy2013nonprofit (city and year FE, models 3–4); @marquis2013golfing (FE check, Table 4); @mayer2025connecting (county and year FE); @shon2024demographic (county and year FE); @mcdonnell2020charity (within-area change models) |
| **Random effects** | Mostly differences between places | @bae2018factors; @marquis2013golfing (main models, lagged count) |
| **Pooled cross-section** | Places, in several years stacked | @benner1992empirical (1982 and 1987); @allard2023volatility (2007–2017); @lecy2013nonprofit (models 1–2) |
| **Single cross-section** | Places, in one year | @corbin1999study; @bielefeld2000metropolitan; @gronbjerg2001community; @saxton2005social; @kim2015socioeconomic; @shapiro2021inequality; @shapiro2026racial; @kim2026interdependence; @jeong2020density; @vanpuyvelde2016determinants; @wu2021geography; @willse2023geography; @wo2018density; @yan2014antipoverty; @peck2008antipoverty; @never2016place |
| **Other** | Growth curves, unconfirmed estimator, or meta-analyses | @mcdonnell2026development; @kim2022prevalence; @lu2020population; @lu2018complementary |

: The studies by research design. Organization-level survival and location studies are not classified. {#tbl-by-design}

:::

# Within-place evidence

## The within-place studies

::: {.table-compact}

| Study | Places and years | Outcome | Fixed effects |
|---|---|---|---|
| @matsunaga2004government | 50 US states, 1992–1999 | Filers per capita (log), NCCS Core | State and year |
| @lecy2013nonprofit | Counties in 331 metros, 1998–2003 | Human-service filers, count, with population and its square | City and year |
| @marquis2013golfing | 100 metros, 1987–2002 (4 waves) | Large nonprofits (\$10M+ assets), count | Metro (robustness model) |
| @mayer2025connecting | US counties, 2010–2016 | Foundings (new registrations) and dissolutions; population offset | County and year |
| @shon2024demographic | 3,129 counties, 2007–2015 | Dissolutions (automatic revocations) | County and year |
| @mcdonnell2020charity | 328 local authorities, England and Wales, 1971–2011 | Charities per 5,000 | Within-area change |
| **Multiverse** | 387 metros (and 925 CBSAs), 2010–2022 | Filers, grassroots, spending; SAMI and other forms | Metro and year |

: Within-place studies compared on this page. {#tbl-within-studies}

:::

Two of the six model *flows* (foundings and dissolutions) rather than stocks. Marquis
et al.'s fixed-effects model covers only very large organizations.

**A caveat on identification.**

- **Little variation within metros.** Slow-moving covariates such as racial
  composition, education and religious structure change little within a metro over a
  decade. Within estimates of them rest on small variation and are noisy.
- **Our own recommendation.** The multiverse's design cards therefore treat metro
  fixed-effects estimates as weakly identified (D3).
- **Better for fast-moving covariates.** Within designs are more credible for
  covariates that move, such as government spending, need and population growth.

That is where this section puts its emphasis.

## Results, panel to panel

Each cell gives the direction of a variable's within-place association with the
nonprofit sector:

- [+]{.r-pos} positive, [−]{.r-neg} negative, [0]{.r-null} not significant or near
  zero, [±]{.r-mix} depends on the outcome or subsector.
- **Entry and exit studies** are signed by their effect on the *stock*: a variable
  that raises dissolutions or lowers foundings is shown as −.
- **Multiverse cells** use the median within-metro partial correlation: ± .05 or
  more is signed, smaller is 0.

The multiverse rows are excluded from the agreement rows.

Column key:

- Need = poverty, unemployment or deprivation; Inc = income or wages.
- Het = racial or demographic heterogeneity.
- GovF = government funding paid to nonprofits; GovP = government size or direct
  provision.
- Dens = existing density or competition.

::: {.table-compact .table-matrix}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-within-results
#| tbl-cap: "Within-place results by variable. Agreement is computed across the literature's within-place studies; the multiverse rows are shown for comparison."
#| output: asis
wr <- rd( "within_results.csv" )
matrix_md( wr, c( "need", "inc", "het", "govfund", "govprov", "dens" ),
           c( "Need", "Inc", "Het", "GovF", "GovP", "Dens" ) )
```


## Variable by variable

**Government provision substitutes for nonprofits within places.**

- **Three of four within studies.** As a place's own government grows, its nonprofit
  sector shrinks relative to it:
  - direct state and local spending [@matsunaga2004government];
  - government wages [@lecy2013nonprofit];
  - government revenue [@marquis2013golfing].
- **The multiverse agrees for grassroots.** State and local government earnings are
  negative within metros for grassroots (−.13), and near zero for filers (−.01) and
  spending (+.01).
- **The exception is entry.** Rising government wages go with more *new
  registrations* [@mayer2025connecting].
  - Those are mostly future grassroots organizations.
  - Combined with the negative grassroots stock in the multiverse, more entry does
    not translate into a larger stock: new organizations may not survive.

Separating entry from survival is the clearest next test (Part 10).

**Government funding to nonprofits complements them.**

- **Within the literature.** Funding paid to nonprofits rises with the sector in both
  within studies that measure it [@matsunaga2004government; @lecy2013nonprofit].
- **In the multiverse.** Medicaid, money paid through providers, is positive within
  metros for spending (+.08) and near zero for counts.
- **Interpretation.** Within places, money flowing to nonprofits expands the size of
  organizations more than their number.

The literature's measure of funding is partly an outcome: grants *received by the
organizations counted*. The multiverse's Medicaid measure is not.

**Organizations follow rising need, but needy places also lose organizations.**

- **Need rises, the sector grows.** Need is positive in three within studies:
  - unemployment [@matsunaga2004government];
  - poverty [@lecy2013nonprofit];
  - deprivation, which its authors call tentative evidence [@mcdonnell2020charity].
- **The multiverse agrees for grassroots.** Poverty is positive within metros for
  grassroots (+.08), near zero for filers (−.02), and slightly negative for spending
  (−.05).
- **Turnover.** Economic hardship raises dissolutions [@mayer2025connecting]. The two
  fit together: within a place, rising need brings new and small organizations, while
  hardship shortens the lives of existing ones. The net effect on the filer stock is
  small.

**Heterogeneity does not raise density within places.**

- **In the literature:**
  - racial heterogeneity is null within states [@matsunaga2004government];
  - rising demographic heterogeneity raises dissolutions within counties
    [@shon2024demographic].
- **In the multiverse:** % nonwhite is negative within metros for both filers (−.10)
  and grassroots (−.08).
- **Interpretation.** Government failure theory's central prediction, that more
  diverse preferences produce more nonprofits, finds no support in within-place
  designs.
- **Caveat.** Composition changes slowly, so these estimates rest on little
  variation (see the caveat above).

**Density dependence holds.** Within counties:

- higher existing density lowers foundings and raises dissolutions
  [@mayer2025connecting];
- competition raises dissolutions [@shon2024demographic].

The multiverse's strongest within-metro term is the population-growth kernel: −.15
for filers and −.19 for grassroots. When a metro grows, its sector lags behind and
catches up slowly. Both point to a sector pulled toward a carrying capacity set by its
place.

**Income diverges, and is thinly tested.**

- **Negative** within states [@matsunaga2004government].
- **Positive** within cities [@lecy2013nonprofit].
- **Positive only for elite-oriented organizations** within metros
  [@marquis2013golfing].

Three studies, three units and three outcomes. No conclusion is warranted.

## Theories tested within places

Each cell shows whether a study's within-place results support a theory:

- [+]{.r-pos} supports, [−]{.r-neg} contrary, [0]{.r-null} null, [±]{.r-mix}
  mixed.
- **Parentheses** mark *implicit* tests: a variable bearing on the theory is in the
  model, but the paper does not frame it as a test. For example, Marquis et al. never
  mention interdependence theory. Yet their fixed-effects model includes government
  revenue, and it is negative within metros: an implicit test that does not support
  interdependence.

Column key:

- **GF, government failure:** heterogeneity raises density; government provision
  lowers it.
- **Int, interdependence:** government funding raises density.
- **Need:** rising need raises density.
- **Sup, supply:** rising resources raise density.
- **SC, social capital:** rising civic participation raises density.
- **Eco, ecology:** density dependence.
- **Elite:** corporate and elite presence raises density.

::: {.table-compact .table-matrix}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-within-theory
#| tbl-cap: "Theories tested in within-place designs. Parentheses mark implicit tests. Agreement is computed across the literature's within-place studies."
#| output: asis
wt <- rd( "within_theory.csv" )
matrix_md( wt, c( "gf", "int", "need", "sup", "sc", "eco", "elite" ),
           c( "GF", "Int", "Need", "Sup", "SC", "Eco", "Elite" ) )
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Notes by study

```{r}
#| output: asis
notes_md( wt )
```
:::

**What within-place tests say about the theories:**

- **Interdependence: supported for funding, not for provision.** Funding paid to
  nonprofits complements them. Government's own provision substitutes. The theory is
  about the first; tests that use government size measure the second.
- **Government failure: half right.** Its substitution prediction holds within
  places. Its demand-heterogeneity prediction does not: heterogeneity is null or
  negative within places, in both the literature and the multiverse.
- **Need: supported within places.** Within places, organizations follow rising need.
  That is the result cross-sections cannot show.
- **Ecology: supported wherever tested within places.** Density dependence and
  carrying capacity are the most consistent within-place results.
- **Supply: divided in the literature, positive in the multiverse.**
  - The literature's three within-place tests measure income, and they diverge:
    negative within states, positive within cities, positive only for elite
    organizations.
  - In the multiverse, education rises with the sector within metros: % BA +.08 for
    filers and +.14 for grassroots.
- **Social capital: only the multiverse tests it within places.** Turnout rises with
  the sector within metros: +.07 for filers and +.10 for grassroots.

## What the within-place evidence supports

| Claim | Within-place support |
|---|---|
| Government money paid to nonprofits goes with a larger sector | **Supported** in two literature studies; in the multiverse for spending |
| Government's own provision substitutes for nonprofits | **Supported** for established organizations in three studies and for the grassroots stock in the multiverse; **not** for new registrations (one study) |
| Rising need brings more organizations | **Supported** in three studies and for grassroots in the multiverse; hardship also raises exits |
| Rising heterogeneity brings more organizations | **Not supported**: null or negative in the literature and the multiverse |
| Sectors are pulled toward a carrying capacity | **Supported**: density dependence in two studies; slow catch-up after growth in the multiverse |
| Rising income brings more organizations | **Unsettled**: three studies, three different answers |
| Rising education and civic participation bring more organizations | **Supported in the multiverse only**: no within-place tests in the literature |

: Claims supported by within-place designs. {#tbl-within-claims}

# Descriptive context: cross-sectional studies

This section also gives the details of every study reviewed, including the
within-place ones.

Most of the literature compares places at one point in time. Those studies cannot
say what changes density, but they describe where nonprofits are and how studies
have measured them. They are summarized here, without adjudicating their signs.

What they consistently describe:

- **Resources and history.** Places with more education, more wealth and a larger
  inherited sector have denser sectors. History, existing density or region is
  positive in four of the five studies that include it.
- **Spending gaps.** Rural, suburban, high-poverty and predominantly Black counties
  have less nonprofit human-services spending per resident [@shapiro2021inequality;
  @shapiro2026racial; @allard2023volatility]. Part of that gap is what size alone
  predicts for spending (see the size discussion below), and part is underprovision.
- **Identity organizations.** Registered and identity-based organizations are more
  common in diverse places, but community foundations are less common there
  [@jeong2020density; @kim2022prevalence; @wu2021geography].

These are descriptions of levels. They matter to a funder benchmarking a place, but
they are not evidence about what an investment would change.

## The ten older studies at a glance

| Study | Data and unit | Outcome | Identification and model | Theories tested |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| @benner1992empirical | NY State Dept. of Labor; 56 New York counties, 1982 and 1987 pooled | Log **employment** by sector and industry | Three equations, three-stage least squares (3SLS), log-linear | Demand heterogeneity, social cohesion, sector interdependence |
| @corbin1999study | 1992 Census of Service Industries, 1990 census and religious census; 285 metros | **Count** of nonprofit social-service establishments (not per capita) | Cross-section OLS; population not in the model; one-tailed tests | Social cohesion, heterogeneity, market failure, resource dependence, philanthropic culture |
| @bielefeld2000metropolitan | 1996 NCCS Core File (990 filers, $25k+); 9 selected metros | Filers per 10,000; provider mix; finances | Spearman rank correlations, no significance tests | Political culture, wealth, generosity, poverty, heterogeneity |
| @gronbjerg2001community | 1999 BMF plus Core; 92 Indiana counties, cross-section | **Registered** 501(c) organizations per 10,000 (all, (c)(3), (c)(4), other) | Cross-section OLS, per capita | Demand, supply, community structure |
| @matsunaga2004government | NCCS Core Files; 50 states (DC excluded), 1992–1999, 400 state-years | **Filers** per 10,000 residents, logged | Two-way fixed effects (state and year), log-log; 2SLS for government variables | Government failure, complementary financing, social cohesion, contract failure |
| @saxton2005social | BMF ruling dates; 284 counties in the 2000 Social Capital Benchmark Survey | **Foundings** of 501(c)(3)s in 2001 | Negative binomial; population as a control; state-clustered SEs | Social capital, organizational ecology |
| @lecy2013nonprofit | NCCS digitized 990s, 1998–2003; counties in 331 MSAs | **Human-service filers**, count | Pooled OLS and two-way fixed effects; population and its square as controls | Government failure vs. interdependence |
| @marquis2013golfing | NCCS Statistics of Income sample (990 filers with $10M+ in assets); 100 metros with 5+ corporate headquarters; 1987, 1992, 1997, 2002 | Next year's count of **large** elite-oriented and social-welfare nonprofits | Random effects with the lagged count (a change model); fixed-effects check; population as a control | Elite and corporate institutional theory |
| @kim2015socioeconomic | 2008 BMF; 3,036 US counties, cross-section | **Registered** 501(c)(3) public charities per 10,000; whole sector and 10 subsectors | Multilevel random intercepts (counties in 49 states), linear per capita | Demand heterogeneity (inequality, diversity), government size, political engagement |
| @bae2018factors | Indiana Nonprofit Employment reports (QCEW); 92 Indiana counties, 2001–2009 | Log total nonprofit **employment** (all 501(c)) | Random effects with year effects; population and its square as linear controls | Government failure, interdependence, social capital |

## Their designs, decision by decision

The studies differ on almost every decision the multiverse varies. Read each column
against the decision cards (Part 6):

::: {.table-compact}

| Study | D1 Population | D2 Unit | D3 Identi­fication | D4 Outcome form | D8 History | D11 Scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ben-Ner 1992 | employment | county (one state) | pooled, 2 years | log level | — | by industry |
| Corbin 1999 | establish­ments | metro | cross-section | **raw count, no population term** | — | social services |
| Bielefeld 2000 | filers | metro (9) | rank correlations | per capita | — | full sector and mix |
| Grønbjerg 2001 | registered (mostly grassroots) | county (one state) | cross-section | per capita | — | by 501(c) type |
| Matsunaga 2004 | filers | state | within (two-way FE) | log per capita | absorbed by FE | full sector |
| Saxton 2005 | foundings (a flow) | county | cross-section | count, population on the right | existing density included | full 501(c)(3) |
| Lecy 2013 | filers | county within MSA | pooled and within (FE) | count, population on the right | absorbed by FE | human services |
| Marquis 2013 | large organizations only ($10M+ assets) | metro (100) | change; within (FE) as a check | count, population on the right | Northeast, 1905 business base | elite vs. welfare |
| Kim 2015 | registered (mostly grassroots) | county (national) | cross-section, state random intercepts | per capita | — | full and 10 subsectors |
| Bae 2018 | employment | county (one state) | panel, random effects | log total, population linear on the right | — | all 501(c) |

: Each study's choice on the decisions that the multiverse finds most consequential. "—" means not included. {#tbl-designs}

:::

The multiverse ranks these decisions by how much they move results (Part 8,
Findings):

- **The three estimand decisions matter most.** Population (D1), identification (D3)
  and unit (D2) each change **20–42%** of verdicts across the 13 covariates: whether a
  covariate is significantly positive, not significant, or significantly negative.
- **The ten studies differ on all three at once.** No two of them share the same
  population, unit and identification.

So the disagreements are the expected result. **Most of the conflicts are not
contradictions. They are answers to different questions.**

::: {.callout-important}
## How studies handle size: is population in the model?

@corbin1999study regresses the *raw count* of nonprofit social-service establishments
in 285 metros on its covariates, with no population term on either side.

- **What the outcome measures.** Establishment counts scale almost one-for-one with
  population (Fact 1), so the outcome is mostly city size.
- **What the covariates pick up.** Any covariate that grows with size comes out
  positive. Corbin's religious diversity is the *number* of denominations, a count
  that rises with size. Its bivariate correlation with the outcome is the strongest
  in the paper (*r* = .70).
- **The opposite case.** @gronbjerg2001community use the same measure, the number of
  denominations, against a *per-capita* outcome, and find it *negative*.

Same measure, opposite signs. The difference is decisions D4 and D6: how the outcome
and the size-scaled covariates handle population. The multiverse shows these
"avoidable error" decisions (predictor form, DV form, log population on the right)
change 13–32% of verdicts.
:::
## Recent and related studies

The ten studies above end in 2018. Since then the field has moved in three
directions:

- **Density and growth studies** now use national data, panels and spatial models.
- **Entry and exit:** a separate literature studies which places gain and lose
  organizations.
- **Location within places:** spatial analyses ask where nonprofits sit, and whether
  that matches need.

The tables below summarize 26 such studies. Unlike the ten, they are **not** compared
coefficient by coefficient. Their outcomes, units and methods differ too much from
ours for that. Instead, the discussion that follows asks whether each strand
strengthens the claims of this page and the multiverse, or competes with them.

**Verification.** Every citation was checked against Crossref.

- **Read in full, or in large part:** studies marked *full*.
- **Abstract only:** the rest. Their findings come from the abstracts, and their
  data details are sometimes incomplete.

Two studies from England and Wales are included because they follow density over 50
years, which no US study does.

### Density and growth

::: {.table-compact}

| Study | Data, unit, years | Outcome (population) | Method | Main finding | Read |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| @shapiro2026racial | NCCS Core 2017; 3,140 US counties | Human-services spending, log per capita | Cross-section OLS | Counties with a larger Black share have less nonprofit human-services spending per resident; the gap is concentrated in the South | full |
| @kim2026interdependence | GuideStar 2003; 2,904 counties | Environmental nonprofits, log count; population as a control | Spatial lag and error model (SARAR) | Educational and racial heterogeneity negative; government grants and spending positive; fiscal centralization negative; strong spillovers between neighboring counties | full |
| @mcdonnell2026development | Charity register; 330 local authorities, England and Wales, 1971–2021 | Charities per 1,000 | Latent growth curves | Density rose to 2001, then plateaued and fell. Trajectories have the same shape everywhere, but level differences persist; middle-deprivation areas are densest | full |
| @allard2023volatility | NCCS 2000–2017; urban and suburban counties | Health and human-services spending per capita and per poor person | Trends; pooled regressions | Suburban safety nets are weaker and more volatile than urban ones, especially in high-poverty and Black suburbs | full |
| @willse2023geography | Park and conservation support nonprofits; counties, 2000–2015 | Whether a county has one | *Not confirmed* | More likely in metro counties with well-educated, liberal residents; unrelated to public parks funding | abstract |
| @kim2022prevalence | Counties, 1995–2015 | Ethnic, cultural and folk nonprofits | County panel | They increase where new immigrant populations grow, unevenly across groups | abstract |
| @shapiro2021inequality | NCCS Core 2013 human-services filers; all US counties | Human-services spending, log per person in poverty (and per capita) | Cross-section OLS with region and controls; state fixed effects as a check | Rural counties spend least, the most rural least of all; the negative poverty association is explained by rurality and region | full |
| @wu2021geography | Service areas of 956 community foundations, 2018; 3,130 counties | Number of foundations serving a county; grants, donations and assets per capita | Hurdle negative binomial | Foundations form in urban, White, homogeneous, high-capital counties; once present, they are more active in diverse and unequal ones | full |
| @lu2020population | Meta-analysis: 37 studies, 491 effects | Sector size, various | Random-effects meta-analysis | Heterogeneity is positively related to sector size, but weakly; age, education, ethnicity, language and religion fit best | full |
| @jeong2020density | BMF 2013; US counties | Registered arts, health and human-services charities, log per 10,000 | Cross-section OLS, state dummies | Government size negative, fragmentation positive; racial and educational diversity and religious adherence positive; for-profit providers co-locate | full |
| @mcdonnell2020charity | Charity register; 328 local authorities, 1971–2011 | Charities per 5,000 | Poisson; within-area change; spatial controls | Density is highest in the least deprived areas, but rises *within* an area as it becomes more deprived | full |

## All studies by population, outcome and form

The table classifies every place-level study on this page on three of the
multiverse's decisions:

- **Population counted (D1):**
  - **Grassroots:** registered organizations that do not file a full return. No
    study isolates them, so the column marks studies of *new registrations*, which
    are mostly future grassroots.
  - **Filers:** organizations filing a Form 990 or 990-EZ, including studies that
    count employers or establishments.
  - **All registered:** the full registered stock, which is mostly grassroots.
- **Outcome measured:** counts, expenses, revenue or assets. Other outcomes are in
  the notes.
- **Form (D4):** how the outcome handles population.
  - **Raw:** no population adjustment, or population entered only linearly.
  - **Per capita:** the outcome divided by population, logged or not, including
    Poisson models with a population offset. All of these impose a scaling exponent
    of 1.
  - **Log, no log P:** a logged outcome with population absent or entered linearly.
  - **SAMI or log with log P:** a logged outcome with log population on the right,
    so the exponent is estimated, or the residual from that fit.

✓ = yes; ? = not confirmed from the paper.

Column key:

- **Population:** Grass = grassroots (new registrations); Filer = filers; All = all
  registered.
- **Outcome:** Cnt = counts; Exp = expenses; Rev = revenue; Ast = assets.
- **Form:** Raw; PC = per capita; Log = log, no log P; SAMI = SAMI or log with
  log P.

**What the table shows:**

- **Per capita dominates.** Thirteen of the 26 classified studies divide by
  population, which imposes a scaling exponent of 1. For *counts* that is close to
  right at the metro level (Fact 1).
- **Per capita misleads for spending.** Spending scales faster than population
  (β ≈ 1.27 across metros, 1.46 across counties), so spending per resident rises
  with size by construction. Every spending study here uses per capita or per poor
  person: @shapiro2026racial, @shapiro2021inequality and @allard2023volatility.
  Their rural and suburban gaps are therefore partly what scaling alone predicts
  for smaller places (D4). Shapiro (2021) finds the *most* populous rural counties
  spend relatively more, which fits that reading. That does not make the gaps
  unimportant to a funder, but it changes their interpretation: some of the gap
  is size, and some is underprovision.
- **No study estimates the exponent.** None uses a SAMI or log population on the
  right, except possibly Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen and Kim, Zhang & Liu (not
  confirmed). The multiverse is the only design here that lets the data decide how
  density scales.
- **Raw counts remain.** Five studies model raw counts with population only as a
  linear control, or not at all. Corbin is the extreme case.
- **Grassroots are never isolated.** Grassroots appear only inside "all registered"
  or as new registrations. Within places, filers and grassroots respond differently
  to government and need, so the population counted changes the answer.
- **Assets are almost never the outcome.** Only Wu (2021) measures assets, for
  community foundations.
# Do the newer studies strengthen our claims, or compete with them?

The question is asked of the within-place evidence first, then of the descriptive
studies.

**Within-place studies: mostly strengthen.**

- **Carrying capacity and persistence.** Density dependence within counties
  [@mayer2025connecting; @shon2024demographic] supports the multiverse's slow
  catch-up after growth and the persistence of density (Facts 2 and 3).
- **Need within places.** Density rises within an area as it becomes more deprived,
  tentatively [@mcdonnell2020charity]. That matches the grassroots result in the
  multiverse.
- **Heterogeneity raises turnover, not density.** Rising demographic heterogeneity
  raises dissolutions within counties [@shon2024demographic]. The multiverse's
  negative within-metro estimate for % nonwhite is consistent with that.
- **Competes: government and entry.** Rising government wages go with more new
  registrations [@mayer2025connecting], while three studies and the multiverse's
  grassroots stock show substitution. The two can both hold if new organizations do
  not survive. That remains the main open question.

**Descriptive studies: context, and three gaps.** The cross-sectional literature adds
three things the multiverse does not cover:

- **Spatial spillovers.** Strong spillovers between neighboring counties
  [@kim2026interdependence; @never2016place]. The multiverse treats metros as
  independent, so a spatial check belongs in its next version.
- **Rural places.** Rural counties outside metro and micro areas, where safety nets
  are thinnest [@shapiro2021inequality]. They are outside the multiverse's units.
- **Who is served.** Where organizations are based is not always where they serve
  [@marwell2026configuring], so density by headquarters can overstate access.

All three are listed in Part 10.

# Synthesis

## How the multiverse fills the gap

**It provides the within-place evidence the literature lacks.** Of 36 studies, six
estimate within-place models.

- Their units differ: states, counties, metros and English local authorities.
- Their outcomes differ: filers, large organizations, foundings and dissolutions.
- So do their years.

The multiverse adds a within-metro design on one dataset, for all three populations
(filers, grassroots and spending) at once, for every defensible measure of each
covariate.

**It shows which within-place results are robust:**

- **Government.** Government funding and government provision move in opposite
  directions within places. The literature's "complement or substitute" debate is
  two different variables.
- **Need.** Within places, rising need goes with more grassroots organizations, not
  more filers.
- **Heterogeneity.** It does not raise density within places for either population.
- **Persistence.** Sectors lag population growth and catch up slowly. Of all
  covariates, this has the strongest within-metro association.

**It is honest about what within designs can show.** Slow-moving covariates vary
little within metros, so their within estimates are noisy, and the design cards
treat metro fixed effects as weakly identified (D3). Fixed effects remove stable
differences between places and common shocks. They do not remove changes that
coincide with the covariate. Within-place estimates are closer to causal than
cross-sections, but they are not causal.

## Shortfalls in the existing literature

1. **Too few within-place designs.**
   - Most studies are cross-sections, and their signs describe differences between
     places shaped by long histories.
   - Only six estimate within-place models, and their units, outcomes and periods
     differ too much to pool.
2. **Within-place designs are short and slow-moving.** Panels of five to eight years,
   with covariates that barely change, leave little variation to estimate from.
3. **The population is unstated or pooled.**
   - Studies count registered organizations, filers, large organizations or new
     registrations, and none isolates grassroots.
   - Within places, filers and grassroots answer to government and need in different
     ways.
4. **Government is measured as size when the theory concerns funding.** Size and
   funding move in opposite directions within places, so the measure determines the
   answer.
5. **Measures carry size or the outcome.**
   - Counts of groups, and logged totals with population entered linearly, carry
     size.
   - Grants received by the counted organizations are partly the outcome.
6. **Stocks and flows are not linked.** Entry and exit studies, and stock studies,
   do not speak to each other, so it is unknown whether conditions that bring new
   organizations also let them survive.
7. **One specification is reported.** The decisions that matter most (population,
   identification and unit) are made silently.

## How the literature should proceed

1. **Make within-place designs the default** for claims about what changes density.
   Report cross-sections as description.
2. **Lengthen panels and favor fast-moving covariates.** Government spending,
   funding, need and population growth vary enough within places to estimate.
   Composition and culture mostly do not.
3. **Use events.**
   - Event studies and difference-in-differences around policy changes, plant
     closures, disasters and hospital conversions.
   - Synthetic controls for single communities.

   These sharpen within-place designs into causal ones.
4. **Name the population.** Report filers, grassroots and spending separately (D1).
5. **Separate government funding from government provision,** and avoid grants
   received by the counted organizations as an explanatory variable.
6. **Link stocks and flows.** Model entry, survival and crossing the filing floor
   together [@mayer2025connecting; @shon2024demographic]. That is how to settle
   whether rising government brings lasting organizations or short-lived ones.
7. **Handle size explicitly,** with log-log models or SAMIs (D4, D6), and use
   measures that carry neither size nor the outcome.
8. **Report the decisions that matter,** in a decision table or a small multiverse.
9. **Build on shared, frozen data** (Parts 2–4), so studies differ only in the
   decisions they mean to test.

**For local foundations and governments,** within-place evidence supports four
statements today:

- **Funding.** Public money paid to nonprofits goes with a larger sector, mainly
  larger organizations.
- **Provision.** When government provides more itself, nonprofits do not grow
  alongside it.
- **Need.** Rising need brings new, small organizations, but hardship also shortens
  their lives.
- **Time.** Sectors respond slowly: growth and investment take years to show up in
  density.

The causal effect of a specific local investment remains unknown. That is the gap
the next generation of within-place and event-based studies should close.
